content: Project Harar invites individuals to contribute to the editing of its page and encourages applications for the role of Editor-in-Chief for this topic. There can be one or more Editors-in-Chief. Additionally, individuals may apply to serve as Associate Editors-in-Chief for specific subtopics. Interested applicants are requested to email their interest, specifying whether they wish to oversee the entire topic or a subtopic, and must attach their CV or a biographical sketch. Overview Project Harar, also known as Project Harar Ethiopia, is a UK-registered charity dedicated to assisting children in Ethiopia who are affected by facial disfigurements. Since its inception in 2002, the organization has facilitated treatment and aftercare for over 500 children and young patients living in poverty and social isolation. Project Harar collaborates with Ethiopian and international specialists, including plastic, oral, and maxillofacial surgeons, to address a variety of conditions. The goal is to restore normal facial function and provide these children with the opportunity to live dignified lives, fully integrated into their home communities. History Project Harar was founded after Jonathan Crown, a London-based chartered accountant and businessman, encountered two young boys, Fhami and Jemal, with facial disfigurements while they were begging in the town of Harar, eastern Ethiopia, in 2001. Deeply moved, Crown spent months organizing a trip to bring the boys to The Gambia, where they underwent complex surgeries aboard the M/V Anastasis, a hospital ship operated by the charity Mercy Ships. Following this initial effort, Project Harar began collaborating with other charities and the Ethiopian healthcare system to ensure that patients could receive treatment within Ethiopia. These treatments are now performed by Ethiopian and volunteer foreign surgeons in hospitals located in Addis Ababa. In 2006, English actor John Hurt became the first patron of Project Harar. In 2007, the organization was featured in two BBC World Service programs focusing on noma and the treatment of patients from remote regions. Later that year, a BBC Inside Out documentary highlighted the treatment of severely affected patients from the Hararghe and Somali regions of Ethiopia by a team of UK medical volunteers organized by the noma charity Facing Africa. Operation Project Harar functions as a health outreach charity, acting as a bridge between individuals who could benefit from facial reconstructive surgery and the centralized Ethiopian healthcare services. Its Ethiopian staff work in remote rural areas, collaborating closely with local health administrators and extension workers to identify and support children with facial disfigurements. These children often face significant stigma and social exclusion. Families are informed about the availability of professional medical care, and if they choose to pursue further assessment for surgery, Project Harar covers all associated costs. This includes transportation, accommodation in the capital city, prescription medications, and other aftercare expenses. A guardian is always arranged to accompany young patients and support them throughout their recovery process. Post-surgery, Project Harar emphasizes the reintegration of children into their communities and family lives. The organization conducts follow-up visits and works to reduce stigma against individuals living with facial disfigurements. By restoring essential facial functions such as chewing, swallowing, speech, salivary continence, and facial expression, as well as improving appearance, many children are given the opportunity to attend school for the first time. Through its collaboration with Ethiopian health services and foreign specialists, Project Harar also contributes to the training of local health professionals, thereby enhancing Ethiopia's surgical capacity. The charity primarily operates in the Oromia Region, including the zones of Misraq (East) Hararghe and Mirab (West) Hararghe, which encompass the towns of Harar and Asebe Teferi. It also extends its services to parts of the Somali Region, including Jijiga, and the chartered city of Dire Dawa. In 2008, Project Harar facilitated the treatment of 290 patients with an income of £114,856. Conditions Treated Project Harar provides assistance to children and other individuals living with treatable facial disfigurements caused by a variety of conditions.
